xmlBinders.basis: JSF faces-config: a managed-bean element binds its managed-bean-name to its managed-bean-class, and the managed-bean resolver makes the whole name visible to EL (a dotted name is not a namespace there).
JSF faces-config: a resource-bundle element in application exposes the bundle named by base-name to EL under its var.

Seam components.xml: a component element in the Seam components namespace registers its class under its name, Seam's EL resolver looks component names up (a dotted name is a namespace), and a component with a name and no class configures the component of that name declared elsewhere, for instance by an annotation.

Spring XML configuration: a bean element directly under beans registers its class under its id and each of the aliases in name, which can be separated by comma, semicolon or space but are not in id; a bean nested in a property or constructor argument is an inner bean and registers no name; a bean built by a factory-method or a factory-bean writes the class of the factory (or none), not the class of what the factory returns, so its target is unknown even when a class is written; a bean with a name and a parent but no class of its own takes the class of the definition its parent names, and any other bean with a name and no class is a definition whose class comes from elsewhere; the root is a beans element in the Spring beans namespace or, in the DTD form, in no namespace, while a beans root in another namespace (the Java EE CDI beans.xml) is not Spring configuration. Spring's EL bridge looks a name up whole, so a dotted name is not reachable from EL.

Spring XML configuration: an alias element directly under beans gives the bean named by its name attribute one more name, written in its alias attribute, which is looked up whole like a bean name and stands for the bean it names.

annotationBinders.basis: JSF ManagedBean annotation: name gives the managed bean's name, which the managed-bean resolver looks up whole; left out, it is the unqualified class name with its first character in lower case.

CDI Named annotation: value is the bean's EL name, and a dotted name is a namespace to the EL resolver (the bean named admin.track is reached by #{admin.track}); left out, it is the unqualified class name with its first character in lower case.
CDI Model stereotype: it is a request-scoped Named bean with the default name, the unqualified class name with its first character in lower case.
Seam Name annotation: value is the component's name, and a component has no default name.
Seam Role annotation: name is one more name the component is registered under, and a role has no default name.

Spring stereotype annotations: value is the bean name; left out, it is the unqualified class name decapitalized the way java.beans.Introspector does, which keeps a name whose first two characters are upper case. Configuration and RestController are stereotypes too, because each is meta-annotated with Component (RestController through Controller) and is scanned like it, and on both value is an alias of the name. ControllerAdvice and RestControllerAdvice are scanned the same way, but their value is the base packages, so they are spring-annotation-advice.

EJB session bean annotations: name on Stateless, Stateful and Singleton is the bean's ejb-name, the name another bean addresses it by (the beanName of EJB); left out, the ejb-name is the unqualified class name as it is written, with no change of case. An ejb-name is not an EL name, so a dotted one is not a namespace.

Spring controller advice annotations, meta-annotated with Component (RestControllerAdvice through ControllerAdvice) and scanned like the stereotypes: value is an alias of basePackages, not a name, and name (Spring 6.1 and later, an alias of the Component value) is the bean name; left out, it is the unqualified class name decapitalized the way java.beans.Introspector does.

expressionLanguages.basis: Unified EL as JSF and JSP evaluate it: #{...} and ${...} in view templates (a classic JSP page is template text, its HTML tags included, which the JSP compiler searches for expressions as a whole; the XML forms are parsed as XML first), with the implicit objects of JSP 2.x and JSF 2.0-4.0 resolved before any named bean (the union of both, as the version in use is not known), and the variables a tag declares local to the page: var and varStatus, the rowIndexVar of the Tomahawk and PrimeFaces data tables, the Facelets ui:param name (not the request parameter name of f:param or c:param), jsp:useBean id, and the expression roots Tomahawk aliasBean gives its alias.

xmlInjections.basis: Spring XML configuration: a property or constructor-arg ref, a ref element's bean, local or parent, an entry's key-ref or value-ref, a lookup-method bean, a replaced-method replacer, and an attribute of the p or c namespace ending in -ref each name another bean that the container supplies to the nearest enclosing bean definition (ref local looks only in the same file and ref parent only in the parent container, which a static reading cannot see); idref is deliberately not a site, because it passes the id of the other bean as a string and does not inject the bean, and lookup-method and replaced-method are method injection, in which the container overrides a method to return the named bean or implements the method by the named bean.

annotationInjections.basis: Spring annotation injection by name: a Qualifier on a field or a parameter and a Resource on a field or a setter method each name a bean that the container supplies to the class it instantiates, so the consumer is a class one of the Spring binders manages (a bean element, or a stereotype annotation), and the name is looked up among the beans of the context that instantiated it, in whichever unit declares that bean; a class no Spring binder manages is not injected by Spring, and its Resource, in an EJB or CDI class, names a JNDI resource instead of a bean.

sites.basis: Spring Qualifier: value on an injected field or constructor or method parameter is the name of the bean wanted; there is no name to default to, an unqualified injection point is injected by type, and on a method it is mostly the qualifier of the bean that an annotated method declares rather than of an injection (only a method that returns nothing, a setter, qualifies what is injected), so a method is not a position this site reads.

Resource in the Common Annotations: name is the bean name; left out, it is the field name, or the property a setter method stands for (the method name after set, decapitalized the way java.beans.Introspector does), and the method name itself for any other method, and when no bean has that default name Spring injects by type instead, so a name taken by default and bound to nothing is not a missing bean.

annotationInjections.basis: Seam annotation injection: In on a field or a setter method of a Seam component has Seam inject the context variable of that name, which is looked up among Seam component names (the Name and Role annotations and components.xml) and not among the other beans that share the el namespace, JSF managed beans and CDI named beans, which Seam does not inject; Seam injects into its own components only, so the consumer is declared by the same binders.

sites.basis: Seam In: value is the name of the context variable; left out, it is the name of the field, or of the property a setter method stands for (the method name after set with its first letter lower case), and no other method has one; a value that starts with #{ is an EL expression that Seam evaluates to get the value, not the name of a component.

annotationInjections.basis: EJB annotation injection by name: the EJB annotation names another enterprise bean by its ejb-name, which the Java EE container looks up among the beans of the application and injects into any class it manages, a servlet, a CDI bean or a JSF bean as much as a session bean, and a static reading has no sure way to tell which classes those are, so the consumer is not required to be managed.

sites.basis: EJB: beanName is the ejb-name of the bean wanted; with none written the container injects by type, and there is no name to default to.
